PLANT GUIDE · FIRESTICKS

Firesticks

Euphorbia tirucalli ‘Sticks on Fire’ — the pencil cactus that catches fire with color

Not a cactus, and barely a leaf in sight: a succulent shrub from Africa built from hundreds of smooth, pencil-thin green stems forking upward in a thicket — and, in strong sun and cool nights, the newest growth flushes yellow, orange, and red from the tips down, the living torches that name the cultivar. Drought-proof and architectural, it carries one firm condition: its milky sap is an irritant, and every cut must be handled with respect.

🔍 Anatomy — Telling It from the Lookalikes

TIRUCALLI
upright pencils forking into a shrub, tips flushing fire — yours
RHIPSALIS
drapes and trails over the pot; clear sap, pearl berries
HATIORA
club-shaped segments stacked joint to joint, like bones

The identification rests on two tests — habit and sap — and the plant in the photo passes both. The stems are perfectly round in cross-section, smooth, and about a pencil’s thickness, forking upward into a standing shrub rather than trailing over the pot’s edge. True leaves are reduced to tiny scales that drop almost as soon as they appear, so the green stems do all the work of photosynthesis; on ‘Sticks on Fire’ the newest stems answer strong light and cool nights by flushing gold, then orange, then red. The decisive test is a cut: this plant bleeds milky white latex — the signature of Euphorbia, and the proof it is no cactus. Cactus sap runs clear, and cacti carry areoles, the little felt pads spines grow from; this plant never forms them. Its closest household lookalikes fail the same tests: Rhipsalis baccifera, the mistletoe cactus, drapes and trails, weeps only clear watery sap, stays a deep even green, carries small white flowers and translucent pearl berries — and is non-toxic. Hatiora salicornioides, the dancing-bones plant, builds its stems from short club- and bottle-shaped segments stacked joint to joint. Neither bleeds milk.

🌿 The names: “pencil cactus” and “firesticks” describe the same plant at two moments — green pencils in the shade, sticks on fire in the sun. Euphorbia honors Euphorbus, physician to King Juba II; the cultivar name, also sold as ‘Rosea’, is pure description. Give the plant sun and a cool night, and the newest stems light up.

🎛️ Conditions — Measured

In the dry tropics of Africa and Madagascar this is a landscape plant — a thicket-forming shrub that, left alone in frost-free ground, becomes a small tree of 15 feet or more, planted for generations as living fencing and now naturalized around the tropics. Its whole design is water economy: leaves shrunk to nothing, stems doing the photosynthesis, roots ready to drink deep and then wait out the dry season. In West Virginia it lives the container life — out into full summer sun to charge its colors, and back indoors well before the first frost.

📋 The Care Card

LightFull sun — at least 6 hours of direct sun is what lights the fire colors. Indoors, give it the brightest south- or west-facing window and turn the pot weekly so the thicket grows evenly. Shade-grown plants stay plain green and stretch thin, pale, and weak.
WaterThe soak-and-dry rhythm. Water deeply until it runs from the drainage holes, then let the mix dry out completely before watering again — roughly every 2–3 weeks indoors in summer, monthly or less in winter. It is very drought-tolerant, and overwatering, not thirst, is what kills it: roots rot in wet soil.
SoilA gritty cactus or succulent mix with extra perlite, pumice, or coarse sand worked in, so water passes straight through. The pot must have drainage holes, and the plant must never stand in a saucer of water.
FeedingLight and optional: a half-strength cactus feed once in spring and once in midsummer is plenty. Nothing in winter, when growth rests.
TemperatureHappy at 60–90°F and tolerant of serious heat. Frost is the hard line: stems are damaged as temperatures approach freezing, and a sustained freeze below about 30°F kills them. Bring container plants in before the first frost — and note that cool autumn nights just above that line, in full sun, are exactly what deepen the fire color before the move indoors.
Pruning & SizeIt grows large — 4–6 feet in a pot over the years, far bigger in the ground. Prune in spring or summer to shape it and check its height. Every cut bleeds latex, so gear up first (see the safety box below) and plan cuts with the sap in mind. The pieces cut away become new plants.
FlowersInconspicuous: small clusters of tiny yellow-green flowers at the stem tips on mature plants in spring and summer. This is a plant grown for its stems and their color, not for bloom.

✂️ Propagation — Cuttings, With Gloves On

  1. Gear up first. Gloves and eye protection, every time — the moment a stem is cut it bleeds milky latex that irritates skin and is genuinely dangerous in eyes.
  2. Cut a healthy stem section about 6–8 inches long with a clean, sharp knife. Work over newspaper; the latex drips before it slows.
  3. Stop the flow. Dip the cut ends in water or blot them — water halts the latex. Wash any sap off skin at once with soap and water.
  4. Callus it. Stand the cutting in a dry, shaded spot for several days to a week, until the cut end has sealed over with a dry skin. Planted wet and open, it rots; planted callused, it roots.
  5. Plant and wait. Set the callused end about an inch deep in dry, gritty cactus mix. Keep it warm and bright, hold off watering for the first week, then water sparingly. Roots form within a few weeks, and fresh pencil tips follow.

🩺 Troubleshooting

Stems wrinkle and shrivelGenuinely thirsty after a long drought. Give one deep drink, drain fully — sound stems plump back within days.
Mushy, blackening stems at the baseRot, from wet soil or the cold-and-wet pairing. Cut back to firm, healthy stem, let the cut callus, and restart in fresh, dry, gritty mix.
All green, no fire colorsNot enough sun, or nights too warm. Move it gradually into more direct light — the newest growth colors first.
Pale, stretched, floppy growthToo little light indoors. Brightest window, rotate the pot, and prune the weak tips back in spring.
Blackened, collapsed tips after a cold nightFrost damage. Prune back to living stem once warmth returns, and protect the plant before the next cold snap.
White cottony tufts in the forksMealybugs — dab off with rubbing alcohol on a swab and recheck weekly. Gloves on: the forks are full of sap-bearing stems.
⚠️

Milky sap — handle with respect. Every stem is full of a white latex that irritates skin and eyes and is toxic if eaten. Wear gloves and eye protection when pruning, taking cuttings, or repotting, and wash any sap off skin immediately with soap and water. If sap gets into eyes, flush with clean water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical care. The ASPCA lists Pencil Cactus (Euphorbia tirucalli) as toxic to cats, dogs, and horses — set the plant where pets and children cannot chew the stems. ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435.

🌿 Reading Your Photo

Give it the sunniest spot available, a gritty mix in a pot with drainage holes, and water on the desert rhythm of soak and dry — then bring it in ahead of the frost. It answers with growth, and then with fire.
